title: Formal and Ideological Concepts of the Rule of Law

content.overview: Formal conceptions of the rule of law focus on generality, publicity, prospectivity and clarity of norms. Ideological or substantive conceptions add requirements of justice, rights and moral content. Indian constitutional practice combines formal legality with substantive constraints through fundamental rights and equality.
content.glance: Classify the claim as formal (process and form of law) or substantive (content and justice); apply the appropriate constitutional standard; avoid collapsing the two without analysis.
content.study: Formal rule of law asks whether power is exercised through known, general, prospective rules. Substantive or ideological conceptions ask whether those rules respect rights and justice. Both matter in India: Article 14 and due process values under Article 21 illustrate substantive constraints, while requirements of legal authorisation and fair procedure illustrate formal ones. Exam answers should keep the distinction clear. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in the Constitution. Do not treat BSA 2023 as the source of this doctrine.

sections.heading: Formal Conception
sections.body: Generality, publicity, prospectivity, clarity and legal authorisation of power.

sections.heading: Substantive Conception
sections.body: Rights, justice and non-arbitrariness as part of the ideal.

sections.heading: Indian Synthesis
sections.body: Constitutional rights and equality give substantive content to legality.

sections.heading: Practical Use
sections.body: Plead formal defects (no legal power, retrospective abuse) and substantive defects (arbitrariness, rights violation) distinctly.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.body: Not every unfair outcome is a rule-of-law violation; identify the precise formal or substantive defect.

provisions.title: Life and personal liberty — fair procedure

examples.title: Formal defect
examples.body: A burden is imposed under a secret unpublished instruction with no legal source. Formal legality fails.

examples.title: Substantive defect
examples.body: A published law authorises action but is applied arbitrarily in violation of Article 14. Substantive rule-of-law constraints are engaged.

hypotheticals.question: Does rule of law only mean written statutes exist?
hypotheticals.analysis: Formal legality also requires generality, clarity and prospectivity; substantive views add rights content.

hypotheticals.question: Does substantive rule of law let courts rewrite all policy?
hypotheticals.analysis: Substantive review is structured by constitutional rights and standards, not free-floating preference.

distinctions.title: Formal vs substantive rule of law
distinctions.left: Focus on form and process of norms
distinctions.right: Focus on content, rights and justice

misconceptions.correction: Substantive review is structured by constitutional rights and standards, not free-floating preference.

cases.name: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Constitution has a basic structure that Parliament cannot destroy.

cases.name: Smt. Indira Nehru Gandhi v Shri Raj Narain
cases.issue: Whether essential constitutional controls can be removed.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Rule of law and essential constitutional limitations cannot be displaced by amendment.
cases.holding: Impugned arrangement invalid to the extent it damaged basic principles.

cases.name: I.R. Coelho (Dead) by LRs. v State of Tamil Nadu
cases.issue: Whether Ninth Schedule protection is unlimited.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Post-Kesavananda Ninth Schedule laws remain subject to basic-structure review.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a formal/substantive rule-of-law problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Classify formal vs substantive claim. II. Apply the matching constitutional standard. III. Avoid collapsing the two. IV. Conclude with precise defect and remedy.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Identify formal or substantive defect; cite Article 14/21 as relevant; seek precise relief.
